t: Digital Ethics, the Law and the Planet
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's topic is Digital Ethics, the Law and the Planet.

It's a big one. We'll cover what ethics means in technology, copyright and licences, crediting your sources, who owns AI content, data protection, the Computer Misuse Act, the environmental cost of tech, and how to debate a tricky case.
Let's start with ethics. Ethics is about the ideas people use to decide what is right and what is wrong.
And here's the key point: legal and ethical are not the same thing. The law is the set of rules made by Parliament. Something can be perfectly legal and still be unkind or unfair.
Like posting an embarrassing photo of your mate without asking. Probably not a crime. Definitely not nice.
Next idea: trade-offs. A trade-off is when you gain something but lose something else. Every technology has them.
Take a smart doorbell camera. The owner feels safer and parcels don't get nicked. But the neighbours and everyone walking past get recorded without being asked.
And those neighbours are stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone affected by a technology, even people who never chose it.
So the big question to ask about any design is not just, does it work? It's, who does it work for, and who does it leave out?
Pause and test yourself. A school moves all homework online. Which pupils might be left out?
Pupils with no laptop at home, or with slow rural broadband. Spotting that lets the school improve the plan, maybe by opening the library after school.
On to page two: intellectual property. That means creations of the mind. Writing, music, art, inventions, logos.
There are a few kinds. Copyright protects creative work like stories, songs, photos, films and computer code. A patent protects an invention. A trade mark protects a brand, like a logo or a name.
In the UK the main law is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act nineteen eighty-eight.
And copyright is automatic. The moment you write that song or save that code, it's protected. No forms, and you don't even need the little c in a circle symbol.
How long does it last? For most books, songs and pictures, the creator's whole lifetime plus seventy years.
But copyright doesn't protect ideas. The idea of a game about building with blocks isn't protected. The actual code and artwork are.
There's also something called fair dealing. It lets you use a small, fair part of a work without permission, for things like private study, review, quotation, teaching, news and parody.
So copying one diagram into your revision notes with the source written underneath? Fair. Uploading a whole film to YouTube for educational purposes? Absolutely not.
Two mistakes to avoid. First, if it's on Google, it is not automatically free to use.
And second, crediting the creator is good manners, but it doesn't give you permission on its own.
So how do you get permission? With a licence. A licence is permission from the owner to use their work, usually with conditions.
If a work says nothing at all, assume all rights reserved. That's the default. You have to ask.
Then there's Creative Commons, a set of free licences built from four building blocks.
B Y means attribution, so credit the creator. S A means share alike, so share your new version under the same licence.
N C means non-commercial, so no making money from it. And N D means no derivatives, so don't change it.
Pause and test yourself. You're making a poster to sell tickets for a games night. Can you use an image licensed C C B Y N C?
No. N C means non-commercial, and selling tickets is commercial.
What about the public domain? That's work with no copyright at all, either because it ran out, like Shakespeare, or because the creator gave it away.
Careful though. Beethoven's music is public domain, but an orchestra's brand new recording of it has its own copyright.
And for software, there's proprietary software, where the code is kept secret and you just buy the right to use it, like Microsoft Office.
And open-source software, where anyone can read, change and share the code. Firefox, Linux and Python are all open source.
Page four is about crediting sources. Plagiarism means presenting someone else's work or ideas as if they were your own.
And that includes swapping a few words in someone else's paragraph. That's not paraphrasing. That's still plagiarism.
To avoid it, use a citation, which is a short note in your text, like BBC, twenty twenty-five, in brackets.
And then a reference list at the end, with the full details of every source.
For a website in Harvard style, it goes: author or organisation, then the year in brackets, then the title, then available at and the web address, and finally the date you accessed it.
Why the accessed date? Because web pages change, so it shows which version you read.
For a Creative Commons image, remember TASL. Title, author, source, licence.
And if you used AI to help, say so. Name the tool, the date and what you used it for. At GCSE you have to acknowledge any AI use in coursework.
Which brings us nicely to page five: AI and ownership. This one is properly debated, so there isn't one right answer.
Generative AI makes new text, images, music and video from a prompt. Some of it is so realistic it's hard to tell from the real thing.
Which can be fun, or it can be used to mislead, like a deepfake video of a politician saying something they never said.
To learn, these AI models are fed training data. Billions of web pages, books, photos and songs, a lot of it copyrighted, and mostly collected without asking.
So question one: who owns what the AI makes? The person who typed the prompt? The AI company? The artists it learned from? Or nobody?

In the USA, courts have said that something made entirely by AI, with no human author, can't be copyrighted. The UK has an older rule about computer-generated works, but in twenty twenty-six the government proposed removing it.
Question two: is it fair to train AI on artists' work? Many artists say no. Their work was used without permission or payment, and AI can copy their style.
Many AI developers say the AI learns patterns, a bit like a student studying art, and doesn't keep copies.
In twenty twenty-five, a big court case in London between Getty Images and an AI company mostly went the AI company's way, but it didn't settle whether training itself is allowed.
Possible compromises include licensing deals where AI companies pay creators, an opt-out for creators, and being open about what training data was used.
Top tip for exam answers here: give both sides with reasons before your own view. Don't present your opinion as a fact.
Page six. Personal data. That's any information that can identify a living person. Your name, address, photo, date of birth.
Some is extra sensitive, like health information or biometrics, such as fingerprints and face scans.
In the UK, including here in Northern Ireland, it's protected by the U K G D P R and the Data Protection Act twenty eighteen.
There are seven principles. Lawful, fair and transparent. Purpose limitation. Data minimisation. Accuracy. Storage limitation. Security. And accountability.
In plain English: be honest, only use it for the reason you said, only collect what you need, keep it correct, don't keep it forever, keep it safe, and be able to prove you follow the rules.
Pause and test yourself. A puzzle app asks for your home address. Which principle is that breaking?
Data minimisation. A puzzle game doesn't need to know where you live.
You also have rights. You can ask for a copy of your data. That's called a subject access request, and they normally have one month to reply.
You can ask for mistakes to be corrected, and in some cases ask for data to be deleted. That's the right to erasure, but it isn't automatic.

And news for this year. The regulator used to be the Information Commissioner's Office, the I C O. On the thirtieth of September twenty twenty-six it became the Information Commission. Same job, same powers.
Page seven. The Computer Misuse Act nineteen ninety. It was passed after two men hacked into a B T system in the eighties and there was no law that clearly covered it.

In simple terms it makes four things illegal. Getting into a computer or account without permission. Doing that in order to commit another crime. Damaging or disrupting a computer. And making or supplying hacking tools.
So using your friend's laptop that they left logged in, to post a silly message? That's unauthorised access. And I was only messing about is not a defence.
Paying a few pounds for a service to crash a rival's game server? That's impairing a computer. Also illegal.
But a security tester who breaks into a bank's network with written permission? Totally legal. That's ethical hacking. The difference is always permission.
Quick memory trick for which law is which. Copying and sharing stuff, that's copyright. Personal data, that's GDPR and the Data Protection Act. Hacking, that's the Computer Misuse Act.
Now page eight, the planet. We talk about the cloud as if it floats in the sky, but it's really data centres. Huge buildings full of servers running day and night.
They need loads of electricity, and lots of them use water to cool the hot servers.

The International Energy Agency estimated data centres used about one and a half percent of the world's electricity in twenty twenty-four, and it could roughly double by twenty thirty, mostly because of AI.
And just across the border, in the Republic of Ireland, data centres used about twenty-two percent of all metered electricity in twenty twenty-four.
Remember those are estimates and they change every year. Always say the source and the year.
Then there's e-waste, thrown-away electrical stuff. The U N reported about sixty-two million tonnes in twenty twenty-two, and only about a fifth was properly recycled.
E-waste can leak lead and mercury into soil and water. And it wastes valuable metals like gold and copper.
Look for the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol. That's the W E E E symbol, and it means don't put it in your normal bin. Take it to a recycling centre.
Devices also need mined metals like lithium, cobalt and rare earth elements, which cost energy and water to dig up, and some mining has been linked to child labour.
And for lots of phones, most of their carbon footprint comes from making them, not charging them. So keeping your phone longer is one of the greenest choices you can make.
Page nine is about estimating. Energy in kilowatt-hours equals power in watts, times hours, divided by a thousand.
Pause and test yourself. A fifty watt laptop is used for four hours. How many kilowatt-hours is that?
Fifty times four is two hundred watt-hours. Divide by a thousand and you get nought point two kilowatt-hours.
The classic mistake is forgetting to divide by a thousand. Remember that these are rough estimates, because real devices and prices vary.

Greener habits: keep and repair devices, buy refurbished, recycle properly, switch off instead of standby, download favourites instead of streaming them again and again, and use AI when it genuinely helps.
And if you end up designing apps one day, sustainable design means efficient code, lighter websites, repairable devices and green hosting.
Finally, page ten. How do you actually decide on a tricky ethical question? You use a decision framework.
Seven steps. Facts. Stakeholders. Options. Benefits and harms. Law and rights. Fairness and the planet. Then decide and justify.
The case study is a school that wants pupils to pay for lunch by scanning their face. Some schools in Scotland actually tried this in twenty twenty-one and paused it after privacy concerns.
The benefit is faster queues. The harm is that a face scan is biometric data. If a password leaks you change it. If your face scan leaks, well, you can't exactly get a new face.
So a justified conclusion might be: don't make it compulsory. If it's used at all, it should be optional, with consent, and cards still available.
And in a class debate, challenge the argument, never the person.
Time for a recap. One: legal and ethical are not the same, and every technology has trade-offs.
Two: copyright is automatic and usually lasts the creator's life plus seventy years. Fair dealing allows small, fair, credited uses.
Three: check the licence. All rights reserved means ask. Creative Commons B Y means credit, N C means no money, N D means no changes, S A means share alike.
Four: avoid plagiarism with citations and a reference list, and always say when you used AI.
Five: the U K G D P R and Data Protection Act protect personal data, and the Computer Misuse Act makes hacking illegal.
And six: the cloud and AI have a real environmental cost, so keep devices longer and recycle them properly.
That's it for this episode. Now go and try the page quizzes to check what you've learned.
Thanks for listening. See you next time!
